findings.description: Summary frontmatter states 'Millions of American workers now take instructions from software' as established fact without citation. Body epistemic flags (line 105) self-identify this as an unattributed scale claim, but summaries display independently of epistemic flags — readers encounter the claim without the qualification.
findings.suggestion: Hedge the summary: 'A growing number of American workers now take instructions from software' or 'Workers across multiple sectors now take instructions from software.' Reserve the specific scale claim for body text where epistemic flags accompany it.
findings.context: summary: "Millions of American workers now take instructions from software — warehouse systems that pace their movements, gig platforms that deactivate accounts without explanation..."

findings.description: Confusing construction: 'None of these practices makes U.S. law automatically illegal.' Reads as 'makes law illegal' rather than the intended meaning 'automatically violates U.S. law.' The phrasing inverts subject and object.
findings.suggestion: Rewrite: 'No U.S. law automatically prohibits these practices' or 'None of these practices automatically violates existing U.S. law.'
findings.context: None of these practices makes U.S. law automatically illegal. Some face regulatory scrutiny under OSHA, the NLRA, or state laws.

findings.description: CTA section links to voter guide blog posts (/2026-03-06-voter-guide-which-senators-could-move, /2026-03-08-voter-guide-contact-your-senator) instead of the /action/ guide. Articles 1, 4, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, and the Optional Protocol post all link to /action/. Articles 6, 7, 8, and 9 link to voter guide posts instead. Inconsistent CTA pattern across the ICESCR series.
findings.suggestion: Standardize CTA sections across the ICESCR series. Use the /action/ guide link (which covers contact methods comprehensively) and optionally add voter guide links as supplementary references. Apply to articles 6, 7, 8, and 9.
findings.context: the voter guide on this site includes [specific senators who could move on ratification](/2026-03-06-voter-guide-which-senators-could-move) and [what you can do right now to make contact](/2026-03-08-voter-guide-contact-your-senator)

findings.description: High-frequency ICESCR-series terms absent from glossary: 'algorithmic management,' 'progressive realization,' 'CESCR' (Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights), 'general welfare.' These appear across 10+ posts in the series. The glossary serves reader comprehension — readers encountering these terms for the first time lack a site-level definition.
findings.suggestion: Add glossary entries for these 4 terms under the 'treaty' or 'enforcement' category. Progressive realization and CESCR warrant entries given their centrality to the entire ICESCR series.
findings.context: Glossary currently has 49 terms. These 4 terms appear in every ICESCR article post but lack definitions accessible through the /glossary page.

findings.description: Purpose claim stated as direct observation: 'the observable effect serves private economic benefit rather than general welfare.' Fair witness discipline distinguishes observation (distributional pattern) from inference (purpose/intent). The phrasing presents a purpose inference as an observed fact.
findings.suggestion: Reframe: 'the distributional pattern favors private economic benefit over general welfare' or 'the observable effect appears to serve private economic benefit rather than general welfare.'
findings.context: When platform companies classify workers as independent contractors to reduce labor costs and expand margins, the observable effect serves private economic benefit rather than general welfare.

findings.description: 'LLM-factors psychology' used as a project-coined term throughout the post but absent from the glossary. The glossary includes 'apophatic-method' (another project-coined term). LLM-factors psychology warrants the same treatment as a novel term readers need defined at the site level.
findings.suggestion: Add a glossary entry for 'LLM-factors psychology' under the 'methodology' category with a definition following the existing glossary style (E-Prime, fair witness).
findings.context: LLM-factors psychology appears in the title, summary, and throughout the body as a novel discipline name coined by the project.

findings.description: CBO projection framed as accomplished fact: 'cut approximately $990 billion (gross) from Medicaid.' The verb 'cut' (past tense) presents a CBO projection of future spending reductions as a realized outcome. The parenthetical '(CBO projection)' provides partial qualification, but the verb tense overrides it — readers parse 'cut' as accomplished fact before reaching the parenthetical.
findings.suggestion: Change 'cut approximately $990 billion' to 'would reduce projected Medicaid spending by approximately $990 billion' or 'projects approximately $990 billion in Medicaid reductions.' Ensure the verb tense matches the projectional status of the CBO estimate.
findings.context: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21, signed July 2025) cut approximately $990 billion (gross) from Medicaid, removing coverage for approximately 10 million Americans (CBO projection)

findings.description: 'trained on billions of creative works' — 'billions' represents an unattributed scale claim. While 'in many cases without compensation' carries appropriate hedging, the quantity claim lacks citation.
findings.suggestion: Either cite a source for the scale estimate (e.g., Common Crawl dataset size, LAION-5B) or use a hedged formulation: 'trained on vast quantities of creative works.'
findings.context: Large language models and image generation systems trained on billions of creative works — text, art, music, code — in many cases without compensation to or consent from their authors.

findings.description: Garbled sentence in summary frontmatter: 'Article 5 ensures that a frequently cited objection to ratification — that it would lower existing labor standards — the treaty itself legally forecloses.' The em-dash structure breaks the grammar — the sentence lacks a complete predicate after the parenthetical. Summaries display independently of body text, so this garbled construction reaches readers directly.
findings.suggestion: Rewrite to: 'Article 5 legally forecloses a frequently cited objection to ratification — that it would lower existing labor standards.' Or: '...the treaty itself legally forecloses the possibility that ratification would lower existing labor standards.'
findings.context: summary: "...Article 5 ensures that a frequently cited objection to ratification — that it would lower existing labor standards — the treaty itself legally forecloses."

findings.description: 'The productivity-pay gap has widened by a factor of 3.5 since 1979' — the EPI link goes to a general page, and the 'factor of 3.5' framing could mislead readers about what the statistic measures. EPI's methodology tracks the ratio of productivity growth to compensation growth, not a simple multiplicative factor applied to the gap itself.
findings.suggestion: Restate precisely to match the EPI finding: 'productivity grew 3.5 times faster than typical worker compensation since 1979' or verify the exact figure and adjust the formulation to match the source methodology.
findings.context: The productivity-pay gap has widened by a factor of 3.5 since 1979 (Economic Policy Institute)

epistemic_flags: Vocabulary findings (f4, f6) based on glossary snapshot at scan time; terms may have been added since
CTA inconsistency (f3) may reflect intentional variation by publication date rather than oversight
Fair witness findings (f5, f7, f8, f10) involve judgment calls about hedging adequacy — reasonable interpreters may disagree on threshold
Template-letters (f7) CBO figure status depends on whether the OBBBA has taken full effect at time of reading — verify current implementation status
